text.p: A bacterium drawn from sewer sludge breathes in toxins from polluted groundwater and gives back harmless ethene gas, scientists reported.

The bacterium, known as coccoid Strain 195, was isolated from sludge at a sewage treatment plant in Ithaca, New York. The sewage treatment plant was created in the days when toxic dry-cleaning solvents and industrial degreasing agents were simply flushed away.

Strain 195 breaks down two specific pollutants -- tetrachloroethene (PCE) and trichloroethene (TCE) -- into ethene gas, which is so non-toxic that it can be used to ripen tomatoes, microbiologist Stephen Zinder said in a telephone interview.
Findings about the bacterium were reported in Friday's edition of the journal Science.
The bacterium works on the toxins through anaerobic respiration, or airless breathing, and completely breaks down these two chemicals, which are both suspected carcinogens.
"It almost breathes pollution," said Zinder of Cornell University, which is in Ithaca, N.Y.
Organisms discovered earlier only took the break-down process halfway, transforming suspected carcinogens into known carcinogens, such as vinyl chloride.
Even though Strain 195 may hold promise for pollution cleanup, scientists need to know more about it, specifically, what kind of environment it needs to survive.
"I'd sort of like to know what kind of diet it likes," Zinder said, noting that such anaerobes -- organisms that do not need air to live -- often work together with other organisms in communities.
"It's used to having a lot of other organisms around it," he said. "The more we purified it, the harder it was to grow because it didn't have its friends around."
Because Strain 195 appears not to be related to any other known bacterium, Zinder also wondered what it breathed before chlorinated solvents entered the groundwater.

To help find a cozy environment for the pollution-eating bug, researchers plan to work with the bacterium at two test sites, a former B-52 airbase in New York state and a working air force base in Nevada.

Such bases, where fighter pilots train, are prime candidates for pollution test sites because they contain pits where crash-and-rescue personnel dumped jet fuel for firefighting practice and then added chlorinated solvents to clean up the oily residue.
